note: Jurisdiction: U.S. federal. Some sources (CRS, Justia, supremecourt.gov PDFs, Federal Register) were blocked or unreadable, so Cornell LII, Wikipedia, law-firm alerts and whitehouse.gov were used instead. Main currency issue: Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026) overruled Humphrey's Executor.

questions.note: Choice 0 is the best answer but out of date: Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026) held FTC commissioners removable at will, so FTC insulation is no longer merely "contested".
Carter Coal (1936) is sometimes counted as a private-delegation case, but the standard count is the two 1935 cases.

Framing is out of date: Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026, 6-3) overruled Humphrey's Executor; a commission with rulemaking and enforcement power has no valid for-cause protection, so the Seila Law multimember question no longer decides the case.
EO 14215 (Feb 18, 2025) extends OIRA review to independent agencies.
Premise is oddly worded (a 2024 filing is timely even on the agency's own 2025 theory), but choice 2 is clearly the Corner Post answer.

claims.claim: Franklin v. Massachusetts (1992) held the President is not an agency under the APA, so presidential action is not reviewable under the APA.
Under the APA a rule is an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect, and an order is the final disposition of a matter other than rulemaking.
Independent agencies such as the FTC have statutory for-cause removal limits whose validity "now sits at the center of a constitutional dispute".
claims.note: Out of date (U.S.): Trump v. Slaughter, decided June 29, 2026 (6-3, Roberts, C.J.), overruled Humphrey's Executor and held the FTC Act's for-cause removal limit unconstitutional. For the FTC the dispute is resolved; the Federal Reserve was treated differently (Trump v. Cook, same day).

claims.claim: The nondelegation doctrine has been enforced to strike down statutes only in Panama Refining and Schechter Poultry, both 1935.
Gundy v. United States (2019): a Kagan plurality of four upheld the SORNA delegation; Alito concurred in the judgment; Gorsuch dissented for three; Kavanaugh later signalled interest.
FCC v. Consumers' Research (2025) upheld the Universal Service Fund under the intelligible principle test and rejected the private-delegation challenge.
Carter v. Carter Coal Co. (1936) invalidated giving private parties power to set wages and hours for competitors.
Humphrey's Executor (1935) upheld protecting FTC commissioners from removal except for inefficiency, neglect of duty or malfeasance, reasoning from quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial powers.
claims.note: Accurate as history; the same source notes it was overruled in Trump v. Slaughter (2026).

claims.claim: Seila Law (2020) barred for-cause protection for a single director with significant executive power, described exceptions for multimember expert bodies and inferior officers with limited duties, and severed the restriction.
The FTC removal case asking whether Humphrey's Executor should be overruled is pending, and the lesson presents the Humphrey's multimember-body exception as current law.
claims.note: Out of date: Trump v. Slaughter was decided June 29, 2026 (6-3) and overruled Humphrey's Executor. The President may remove at will officers who exercise executive power, including multimember commissioners. Companion case Trump v. Cook (5-4, same day) left Fed Governor Cook in office while her case continues. The lesson body and worked example need rewriting.

claims.claim: Trump v. Wilcox (2025) stayed reinstatement of NLRB and MSPB members and described the Federal Reserve as a uniquely structured, quasi-private entity.
Lucia v. SEC (2018) held SEC ALJs are officers whose appointment by agency staff violated the Appointments Clause.
EO 12866 (1993), successor to EO 12291 (1981), has OIRA review significant rules with cost-benefit analysis.
In 2025 an executive order directed independent agencies to submit significant rules for presidential (OIRA) review.
claims.note: EO 14215, signed Feb 18, 2025; excludes Fed monetary policy. After Trump v. Slaughter (2026) its legal footing is stronger than "contested" suggests.

claims.claim: The CRA was used successfully only once before 2017; a disapproved rule may not be reissued in substantially the same form without new statutory authority; CRA determinations are not judicially reviewable.
INS v. Chadha (1983) held a one-house veto unconstitutional for bypassing bicameralism and presentment; Jackson's Youngstown concurrence set out three categories of presidential power.
A final rule ordinarily takes effect no sooner than 30 days after publication (553(d)), with exceptions such as rules granting an exemption or relieving a restriction.
claims.note: 553(b) now also requires a 100-word internet summary of a proposed rule (2023 amendment), which the lesson omits.

claims.claim: Vermont Yankee (1978) held courts may not impose procedural requirements beyond those in the APA, Constitution or other statutes.
Long Island Care at Home v. Coke (2007) applied the logical outgrowth test while upholding a rule.
The APA treats repeal of a rule as rulemaking.
claims.note: 551(5) defines rule making as formulating, amending, or repealing a rule.

claims.claim: Section 553(a) exempts military or foreign affairs functions and matters relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits or contracts.
Good cause exception: the agency must find, and incorporate the finding and a brief statement of reasons in the rule, that notice is impracticable, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest.
Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association (2015) held notice and comment is not required to change an interpretive rule, rejecting the D.C. Circuit's Paralyzed Veterans doctrine.
Allegheny-Ludlum (1972) and Florida East Coast Railway (1973) held that "after hearing" alone does not trigger sections 556-557.
Section 557(d) bars ex parte communications relevant to the merits between interested persons outside the agency and decision-makers in formal proceedings.
The Negotiated Rulemaking Act of 1990 supplements, and does not displace, section 553.
ALJs may be removed only for good cause established by the Merit Systems Protection Board.
claims.note: The statute still reads this way; whether ALJ removal protections are constitutional is open after Free Enterprise Fund, Jarkesy and Slaughter.

claims.claim: Withrow v. Larkin (1975): combining investigative and adjudicative functions does not by itself violate due process; presumption of honesty and integrity.
Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) three-factor test; no pre-termination evidentiary hearing required for disability benefits.
SEC v. Jarkesy (2024): Seventh Amendment requires a jury when the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud; public rights exception inapplicable.
Roth (1972) requires a legitimate claim of entitlement; Goldberg v. Kelly (1970) required a pre-termination evidentiary hearing for welfare.
Bi-Metallic (1915): no hearing required when the board raised the valuation of all taxable property in Denver by the same percentage; contrasted with Londoner.
Chenery I (1943): a court may uphold agency action only on the grounds the agency invoked; Chenery II (1947): the choice between rule and adjudication lies in agency discretion.
Bowen v. Georgetown University Hospital (1988): agencies may not issue retroactive rules unless Congress expressly authorizes it.
Bennett v. Spear (1997) two-part finality test: consummation of decision-making, and rights/obligations determined or legal consequences flow.
Heckler v. Chaney (1985): non-enforcement decisions are presumptively unreviewable, rebuttable where the statute provides enforcement guidelines.
Norton v. SUWA (2004): 706(1) compels only discrete action the agency is legally required to take; Overton Park: the committed-to-discretion exception is very narrow.
Abbott Laboratories: strong presumption of reviewability, overcome only by clear and convincing evidence of congressional intent.
State Farm (1983) grounds for arbitrary and capricious review; the rescission failed for not considering an airbag-only alternative.
FCC v. Fox (2009): the agency need not show the new policy is better, but must show awareness of the change, give good reasons, and account for serious reliance interests.
Ohio v. EPA (2024) stayed the EPA rule because the agency likely failed to respond reasonably to comments about how the rule would work with fewer states.
Department of Commerce v. New York (2019) rejected the contrived VRA rationale for the census citizenship question; Universal Camera requires whole-record review.
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024): plaintiffs who did not prescribe or use mifepristone lacked standing; speculative causal chain; federal conscience protections.
United States v. Texas (2023): states lacked standing to challenge immigration enforcement priorities.
TransUnion v. Ramirez (2021): a bare statutory violation is insufficient; class members whose files were disseminated had standing, others did not.
Abbott Laboratories (1967): two-part ripeness test of fitness and hardship; labeling regulation challenged pre-enforcement.
Darby v. Cisneros (1993): no exhaustion of optional appeals under the APA when not required by statute or rule and the action is final and operative.
Axon Enterprise v. FTC (2023): structural constitutional challenges may be brought in district court.
Laidlaw (2000) voluntary cessation standard; Corner Post (2024): an APA claim accrues when the plaintiff is injured.
Skidmore (1944): weight depends on thoroughness, validity of reasoning, consistency, and power to persuade.
Chevron (1984), Stevens, J., upheld the EPA bubble concept; step one asks whether Congress directly spoke to the precise question; step two asks about permissible construction.
Mead (2001) limited Chevron to interpretations issued under delegated force-of-law authority; tariff classification letters get Skidmore; Christensen (2000) denied Chevron to opinion letters.
Brand X (2005): an agency reading can override a prior judicial construction unless the court held the statute unambiguous.
claims.note: The page opened did not state the rule; not confirmed against a source.

claims.claim: Brown & Williamson (2000) and King v. Burwell (2015) declined deference on questions of vast economic and political significance; in King the Court decided the question itself.
Loper Bright (2024), decided with Relentless, overruled Chevron "by a vote of six to three"; Roberts, C.J.; an NMFS rule required fishermen to pay for observers.
claims.note: Minor imprecision: Loper Bright itself was 6-2 (Jackson recused); Relentless was 6-3.

claims.claim: Prior Chevron-based holdings remain subject to statutory stare decisis; Skidmore respect remains; express delegations are policed for boundaries and reasoned decision-making.
McLaughlin Chiropractic v. McKesson (2025): district courts in enforcement proceedings are not bound by the FCC's TCPA interpretation under the Hobbs Act.
Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (2025) called for substantial deference to agencies on NEPA review choices.
claims.note: Decided May 29, 2025, Kavanaugh, J.; Gorsuch recused.

claims.claim: Kisor v. Wilkie (2019) kept Auer but limited it (genuine ambiguity, authoritative, expertise, fair and considered judgment); four Justices would have overruled Auer.
claims.note: A search found no 2025-26 Supreme Court decision overruling Kisor, but its current status was not confirmed against a page.

claims.claim: Biden v. Nebraska (2023): the HEROES Act power to "waive or modify" did not authorize cancelling about $430 billion in student debt.
West Virginia v. EPA (2022) applied the major questions doctrine to generation shifting, an unheralded power in a long-extant statute.
FOIA requires a determination within 20 working days; review in district court is de novo with the burden on the agency.
Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader (2019) defined confidential under Exemption 4 without a competitive-harm requirement.

The 2016 amendments added a foreseeable harm standard and limited the deliberative process privilege to records under 25 years old; Sears (1975) excludes final opinions (working law) from Exemption 5.
DOJ v. Reporters Committee (1989): compiled rap sheets on private individuals may be withheld; FOIA's purpose is to show what the government is up to.

The Sunshine Act covers agencies headed by a collegial body of two or more members, a majority presidentially appointed with Senate confirmation; it has ten exemptions; closing a meeting requires a recorded vote.
The Privacy Act permits disclosures required under FOIA (552a(b)(2)).
FACA (1972); Public Citizen v. DOJ (1989) read "utilized" narrowly.
Presidential records become subject to FOIA five years after the President leaves office, subject to restrictions.
claims.note: Restrictions may last up to 12 years.
